The negative current density peak in the cyclic voltammetric curve was the copper deposition peak, which represented the ability of copper ions to be reduced to copper and deposited. While, the positive current density peak was the copper stripping peak, whose area represented the ability of the deposited copper to be oxidized to copper ions. The peak area of the copper stripping peak was positively correlated with the peak area of the copper deposition peak. surface_text: With the rapid development of electronic products, advanced fabrication technologies for high-density interconnect (HDI) in the printed circuit board (PCB) are widely applied in 5 G communication, energy devices, wearable devices, and other booming fields [1–3]. Metallization of through-hole (TH) is one of the core technologies to realize the conduction of different layers in HDI-PCB [4,5]. Acidic sulfate copper electronic plating is the most universal process for the metallization of TH [6–9]. TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging and TH void-free copper filling are the two common metallization technologies. For the TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, only a homogeneous and conformal copper coating (about 20 µm) on its side wall is needed [10–14], then epoxy resin is used to fill the TH. For the TH void-free copper filling technology, copper coating is fully filled inside the TH without any void. It is worth noting that TH may crack under long-term heating due to the different thermal expansion coeffi cient between the resin and copper, resulting in the blocked signal transmission. Therefore, compared with TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, TH void-free copper filling technology behaves the advantages of higher reliability and better signal transmission quality. Nowadays, with the acceleration of communication speed, more heat is generated when the signal processing, the copper void-free filling of TH has therefore been widely employed for improving the heat dissipation efficiency.

Copper electrodeposition in high-aspect-ratio through-holes (THs) is the core technology for achieving interlayer electrical interconnection in multilayer PCBs. surface_text: Electroplating is a core technology in high-end chip manufacturing, with its technical challenges centered on achieving voidfree filling of metal coatings within micro- and nanoscale trenches and vias. Copper, the current mainstream interconnect material, can no longer meet the performance and reliability demands posed by the continuous reduction in interconnect dimensions. In contrast, cobalt ofers superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, making it a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of cobalt interconnect technology in chip manufacturing. It examines the electrochemical behavior and interactions of cobalt ions, boric acid, and additives, summarizing the cobalt filling efects and associated mechanism models under diferent process compositions. The discussion also highlights advanced in situ electrochemical characterization technologies to investigate the synergistic and antagonistic efects of various plating bath components, the influence of pH, temperature, and additives on cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Furthermore, the paper explores annealing treatments for cobalt coatings, emphasizing their role in optimizing performance.

surface_text: Electroplating is a critical technology in high-end electronic manufacturing, including integrated circuits. As interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, copper electroplating is increasingly unable to meet the required performance and safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt electroplating, current research has primarily focused on the electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias, along with proposed filling mechanisms. However, several key aspects remain insuficiently explored. These include the specific actions and synergistic/antagonistic interactions of components such as boric acid and additives in the plating bath, the mechanisms by which pH, temperature, and individual bath components influence cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Future research directions should prioritize the development and application of advanced in situ techniques, including morphological, spectroscopic, and energy spectroscopic, to address these challenges. Clarifying these mechanisms will be essential for advancing cobalt electroplating as a viable interconnect technology in next-generation chip fabrication.

surface_text: In advanced electronic manufacturing, additives play a pivotal role in achieving high-quality metal interconnect by enabling precise pattern filling during electrodeposition. Currently, due to complex mechanisms, vast molecular spaces and lack of predictive models, the development of additives still relies on inefficient trial-and-error methods. In this work, a machine learning (ML)-based data-driven framework is developed to accelerate the discovery of cobalt electrodeposition additives. Focusing on molecular adsorption dynamics at the cobalt elec trolyte interface during electrodeposition, this work employs quantum chemical properties to guide the construction of machine learning models for identifying molecules with ideal adsorption potential. Bayesian optimization is employed to optimize model accuracy by tuning hyperparameters, and SHAP analysis provides interpretable chemical insights. Three novel additives are identified, which are 2-aminopyrazine (APZ), 1-methylimidazole-4,5-dicarbonitrile (MIDCN), and 2-amino-4-ethylpyridine (AEP). Electrochemical and electroplating validation confirms that all additives exhibit strong inhibition effects, enabling grain refinement that reduces cobalt film surface roughness below 10 nm $R _ { \mathrm { a } } ,$ with the optimal performer achieving 4.58 nm $R _ { \mathbf { a } } .$ . Furthermore, superconformal filling of through‑silicon vias (TSVs) with aspect ratios >5 is achieved. This work establishes a machine learning-based data-driven strategy as an effective tool for accelerating the discovery of highperformance electrodeposition additives. The identified additives provide new insights into industrial metalli zation solutions for scaled-down nodes.

surface_text: In recent years, many studies have focused on the development of additives for cobalt superconformal electrodeposition and the underlying superfilling mechanisms [11–16]. It has been found that molecules influence the electrode process through their adsorption and interactions with the metal surface [17]. These interactions can be eluci dated by Frontier Molecular Orbital (FMO) theory [18], where a higher highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy indicates a stronger electron donation capability, while a lower lowest unoccupied molec ular orbital (LUMO) energy suggests a greater tendency to accept electrons. Additionally, within the framework of the Hard-Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) principle [19], metallic cobalt $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 0 } )$ is classified as a ‘soft acid and therefore exhibits a preferential affinity for ‘soft bases’ — molecules characterized by a narrow HOMO-LUMO gap (ΔE), as chemical hardness $\boldsymbol \eta \approx \varDelta \mathrm { E } / 2$ . Consequently, in the electrodeposition field, ΔE has been considered as a practical criterion for identifying promising additives [20], as molecules with smaller ΔE values generally exhibit stronger adsorption affinity toward the metal surface and thus exert more significant regulatory effects on the electrodeposition process [21–24]. An et al. [25] demonstrated a strong correlation between ΔE and both calculated adsorption energies and electrochemically measured inhibition ability, successfully applying this metric to identify Methylene Blue as a promising candidate for Cu electroplating.

surface_text: Finding effective additives is a challenge in the field of electrode position. Due to the absence of established screening criteria and the vastness of the chemical space of organic compounds, the process of discovering additives through traditional experimental trial-and-error methods resembles searching for a needle in a haystack and is both time-consuming and resource-intensive [31]. Quantum chemical prop erties enable the prediction of adsorption propensity, thereby accelerating additive screening [13]. However, DFT calculations for numerous molecules often require substantial computational resources and time. Therefore, a much more effective and cost-friendly screening method is essential for achieving high-efficiency screening of additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition. With the accumulation of databases in materials science, machine learning and data-driven strategies have made significant progress in materials discovery [32], property prediction and experiment optimization [33] by uncovering the statistical patterns embedded within extensive datasets and constructing quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) models [34–36]. The combination of first-principles calculations with machine learning is anticipated to enhance the prediction of material properties, thereby expediting the design and discovery of new materials [37] and has been successfully applied to the screening of electrolyte additives of Zn-ion batteries recently [38].

surface_text: To address these copper damascene extendibility issues, alternative metals, such as cobalt, are being actively explored for fill in smaller line dimensions (1-2). In terms of bulk resistivity, copper is significantly superior to cobalt. However, cobalt may not require a barrier layer, which frees up space within the feature for more metal. Because of the difference in barrier thickness, there may be a cross-over at narrow line widths such that a cobalt line will be less resistive than an equivalent copper line (3). Another benefit of removing the barrier is that the features are more open, decreasing the risk of discontinuous seed or pinch-off. Increasing the relative amount of metal within a line should also be advantageous for electromigration, as more metal would have to move to create a void. Additionally, the higher melting point of cobalt with respect to that of copper should lead to improved electromigration performance (1-2).

surface_text: Superconformal cobalt fill does not follow the conventional damascene process, with suppressors, accelerators, and levelers. Rather, it can be achieved using a single organic additive. Previous studies have investigated the effect of various additives on cobalt fill in sub-micrometer trenches and through-silicon vias (4-6). Fill is typically attributed to a potential-dependent suppression effect that results in an S-shaped negative differential resistance. However, this mechanism may not hold for very small dimensions, on the order of tens of nanometers, as the ability to bifurcate into active and passive regimes is dependent on electrode dimensions (7-8).

surface_text: Electroless-plated cobalt alloys with tungsten typically exceeding 5 at.% are the common barrier materials for copper metallization. As cobalt is a new interconnect material for advanced microchips, it is worth studying the advanced cobalt-interconnect metallization process that involves extremely diluted cobalt-tungsten (CoW) alloys with an eliminated impurity resistivity and enhanced electromigration reliability. To this aim, we fabricated three different CoW nanolines with 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.% of W using an electroless process, and examined their electromigration behaviors under accelerated stressing conditions, using Co lines as a control. All three W contents, especially 0.06 at.%, mitigate Co electromigration. The mechanism for the electromigration mitigation is due to an improvement of the film s nanomechanical and surface wetting properties, as well as grain-structure refinements. A full account of the relationship between the film properties, grain structures and electromigration testing results is given, reasonably explaining the cause of the reliability optimization.

surface_text: Copper is the conventional material for metal interconnect in very large scale integration (VLSI). However, as the process node develops from 180 nm to a remarkable 7 nm [1,2], interconnect sizes continue to shrink, resulting in high resistance and high resistance–capacitance (RC) delay [3–5]. The reason is that copper has a relatively large electron mean free path (39 nm) and needs a relatively thick barrier layer to inhibit electron migration [6,7]. Cobalt is a promising alternative material with an average electron free path of approximately 10 nm and low electron migration [8,9]. Therefore, at the same nanometer scale, cobalt has lower resistance and smaller RC delay [10,11]. The key to replacing copper with cobalt is to be able to produce high-quality cobalt interconnects.

surface_text: In this study, a superfilling mechanism was proposed, in which superfilling was achieved by regulating the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. Organic additives containing carbon–carbon triple bonds and oxygen-containing functional groups (BOZ, BEO, and BDE) were examined. The molecular activity and electrochemical behavior analysis revealed that BOZ and BEO exhibited stronger adsorption capabilities on the cobalt surface compared to BDE, owing to their carbon–carbon triple bonds. XRD results indicated that after the addition of BOZ, BEO, and BDE, the cobalt grain size significantly increased. XRD results and adsorption energy calculations demonstrated that the strong adsorption of BOZ and BEO on the (100) and (101) planes of hexagonal close-packed cobalt (HCP\_Co) promoted a preferred orientation along the (002) plane of HCP\_Co. The adsorption energy of BOZ, BEO, and BDE were −10.39 eV, −22.62 eV, and −8.43 eV, respectively. Cobalt superfilling into micro-size trench was achieved by using BDE molecules as additives with an absorption energy of 8 eV. Additives with an extrahigh adsorption energy may inhibit the deposition rate of Co equally both on top and at the bottom of the trench, which cannot benefit from superfilling. However, additive molecules with a suitable adsorption energy may inhibit the Co reduction reaction more strongly on top of the trench than at the bottom, because of the additive molecule concentration gradient caused by mass transport and additive consumption during electrodeposition.
